html:
Zanzibar and Pemba became the world's main source of cloves in the 19th century, after the sultan of Oman moved his court to Zanzibar in 1840, and the plantations were worked by enslaved Africans.

Said bin Sultan encouraged Arab settlers to plant cloves, and the town of Zanzibar grew into the great market for slaves and ivory brought from the interior by caravans, such as those of Tippu Tip. Tens of thousands of captives passed through it each year at the peak, many kept on the islands, others shipped to Arabia and beyond.

Under British pressure the slave market closed in 1873, a story told at Christ Church, and slavery itself was abolished on the islands in 1897. The divide between Arab landowners and Africans led to the revolution of 1964, part of the history of the Omani Empire.
